stages.title: Check your quiz has what it needs

screens.title: Check your quiz has what it needs before you code the rest
screens.goal: Before I code the rest of the quiz, I check I have the question 4 and 5 panels, the Return button, question 3's code and the two things in Global.cs.

blocks.p: A few things need to be done before you can code the rest of the quiz. This screen checks them.

check.what: Open frmQuiz in the Design tab. Does question 4 have a group box, four radio buttons and a Check button?
check.how: In my example it is the panel on the right of the middle row. In yours, look for the panel with the radio buttons.

check.what: Does question 5 have a number box and a Check button?
check.how: In my example it is the wide panel along the bottom. Yours may be somewhere else. Look for the number box.

check.what: Is there a Return button in the score panel?
check.how: In my example it is near the bottom of the tall panel on the left. Yours is in your score panel.

check.what: Double-click question 3's Check button. Is there code between its two curly brackets?
check.how: The code tab opens at the code behind that button. Lines between the curly brackets mean yes.

check.what: Open Global.cs. Are quizScore and quizTaken in it? quizScore counts the right answers. quizTaken remembers whether the quiz has been done.
check.how: Solution Explorer is on the right. Double-click Global.cs to open it. Look for the two lines with those names.

box.title: Not sure where to look?
box.text: Solution Explorer is on the right of Visual Studio 2019. It lists every form. Double-click frmQuiz to see it in the Design tab. Right-click it and choose View Code to see its code.

stages.title: Make only question 1 work when the quiz opens

screens.title: Meet the Load event: code that runs when the form opens
screens.goal: A Load event is code that runs by itself the moment the form opens, before anyone clicks anything.

blocks.p: The quiz has a problem right now. When it opens, all five questions can be clicked, in any order.
You want only question 1 to work at the start. For that you need code that runs the moment the form opens.

words: Code that runs by itself the moment the form opens, before anyone clicks anything.

blocks.intro: Four new things in this chapter. Click any marked word to see what it means.

blocks.p: That code is called a [[Load event|0]]. You have not met one yet. This is the first time you will use one.

drawn.alt: The quiz form slides in. A code card lights up under it with the words runs now.
drawn.say: The quiz form opens. Its Load event runs straight away. Nobody has clicked anything.

blocks.p: Every form can have a Load event if you want one. The quiz needs one, so that is where you write your first.

blocks.watch: A Load event is not a button. Nobody clicks it. It runs by itself when the form opens.

screens.title: Make the Load event by double-clicking the form itself
screens.goal: To make a Load event I double-click the form itself, not a control on it, and Visual Studio writes frmQuiz_Load for me.

blocks.p: Visual Studio makes the Load event for you. All you do is double-click the form itself.

screens.title: Only question 1 can be clicked when the quiz opens
screens.goal: When the quiz opens, question 1 works and questions 2 to 5 are switched off and grey, so they get answered in order.

blocks.p: Here is what the quiz should look like the moment it opens.

flow.say: Question 1 is switched on. Questions 2, 3, 4 and 5 are switched off and grey. The score panel is on.

blocks.p: Each question sits in its own panel. A switched-off panel goes grey, and nothing in it can be clicked.
So the Load event has one job. Switch off the four panels for questions 2, 3, 4 and 5.
Later, when a question is answered, its panel switches off and the next one switches on. You code that in stages 3 and 4.

blocks.watch: Count them: four panels to switch off. The Return button gets hidden too, until the quiz is over.

screens.title: Type the code that switches off questions 2 to 5
screens.goal: In frmQuiz_Load I set Enabled to false on the four panels and Visible to false on the Return button.

blocks.p: Now you type the Load event's code: four panels switched off and one button hidden.

code.title: The quiz's Load event
code.where: between the curly brackets of frmQuiz_Load, in frmQuiz.cs
partLines: Visual Studio wrote these two lines

Switch off questions 2 to 5
The line that starts with two slashes is a note for you. The computer skips it. Then one line per panel. Enabled = false switches the panel off and turns it grey.
Hide the Return button

stages.title: Mark question 4, the one with radio buttons

screens.title: How your code can tell which radio button is chosen
screens.goal: rbB.Checked is true when B's dot is filled in, and an exclamation mark in front means NOT.

blocks.p: Question 4 has four radio buttons. Only one can have its dot filled in.
Your code needs to know which one. Every radio button has [[.Checked|1]]. It is true when the dot is filled in.

code.title: Two ways to ask a radio button
partLines: Is B chosen?
True when the dot of rbB is filled in.
Is A NOT chosen?
The exclamation mark means NOT. True when the dot of rbA is empty.

blocks.p: In my example the radio buttons are called rbA, rbB, rbC and rbD. Yours have the names you gave them.

blocks.watch: An exclamation mark in front means NOT. Read !rbA.Checked as: A is not chosen.

screens.title: Stop if no radio button has been chosen
screens.goal: If none of the four dots is filled in, show a message and use return to stop, so nothing else runs.

blocks.p: What if the pupil clicks Check without choosing an answer? An empty answer should not be marked.
So the first thing the Check button does is look at all four dots. If none is filled in, it shows a message and stops.

code.title: Question 4's Check button, part 1 of 3
code.where: between the curly brackets of btnCheck4_Click, in frmQuiz.cs
partLines: Visual Studio wrote these two lines
Leave them as they are. Your code goes between the curly brackets.
given
No dot filled in? Show a message and stop
The if line asks: are all four dots empty? If they are, a message pops up. Then return stops the code here.

blocks.p: [[return;|2]] means stop here. When nothing is chosen, nothing under that line runs.

drawn.alt: A stop sign drops onto the return line of the code.
drawn.say: The stop sign lands on return. Nothing under this line runs.

blocks.watch: Each && means AND. All four dots must be empty for the message to show.

screens.title: Add 1 to the score if the answer is right
screens.goal: If the right radio button is chosen the score goes up by 1 and the group box turns green, otherwise it turns red.

blocks.p: Now the real marking. If the right dot is filled in, the score goes up by 1. If not, the box turns red.

code.title: Question 4's Check button, part 2 of 3
code.where: between the curly brackets of btnCheck4_Click, in frmQuiz.cs
partLines: Right answer: score up by 1, box goes green
If rbB is chosen, 1 is added to Global.quizScore. The label shows the new score. The group box turns green.
Wrong answer: box goes red
Any other dot turns the group box red. The score stays as it was.
code.yours: In my example the right answer is the second radio button, rbB. Look at YOUR question 4. Which of YOUR radio buttons is the right answer? Use that one's name.

stages.title: Send the score back to the data entry form

screens.title: Code the Return button
screens.goal: The Return button sets quizTaken to true in Global.cs, closes the quiz and opens a new data entry form.

blocks.p: The Return button takes the pupil back to the data entry form. But first it needs to leave a note.
When a form closes, it forgets everything. Global.cs does not forget. It remembers things for the whole program.
Global.quizTaken is one thing in Global.cs. It is false until the quiz is taken. The Return button sets it to true.

steps.do: In the Design tab, double-click the Return button in the score panel.
steps.see: The code tab opens at btnReturn_Click, empty between the curly brackets.

code.title: The Return button
code.where: between the curly brackets of btnReturn_Click, in frmQuiz.cs
partLines: Visual Studio wrote these two lines
Leave them as they are. Your code goes between the curly brackets.
given
Leave the note, close, go back
Global.quizTaken becomes true. this.Close() closes the quiz form. The last line makes a new data entry form and shows it.
Visual Studio wrote this line
This curly bracket is the end. Your code goes above it.
given

blocks.watch: The order matters. Leave the note first, then close, then open the data entry form.

screens.title: Why the data entry form still says Quiz not taken
screens.goal: After Return, the data entry form comes back fresh and has not read Global.cs yet, and chapter 8 fixes that.

blocks.p: Press Return and the data entry form comes back. Its quiz panel still says Quiz not taken yet. The name boxes are empty.
That is fine. Nothing is broken. The note is in Global.cs. The data entry form has not read it yet.

drawn.alt: The fresh data entry form on the left, Global.cs on the right with quizTaken set to true.
drawn.say: The fresh data entry form on the left. Global.cs on the right, with quizTaken set to true.

blocks.p: In chapter 8 the data entry form gets its own Load event. That Load event reads the note when the form opens.

blocks.watch: Do not try to fix this now. Chapter 8 is where it gets fixed.
